exit_trigger: Return on equity falling below 15% in a sustained way, signaling moat erosion; Evidence that clients are pushing down billing rates or cutting outsourced labor because of automation; Negative operating cash flow or management capital allocation that destroys value; Price above 1.5x intrinsic value
rationale: I don't own Accenture, so the question is whether to start. On the numbers in front of me it looks cheap: roughly $252 a share against a conservative owner-earnings value of about $438, with five-year average ROE near 27% and debt-to-equity of 0.32. But a 43% discount on a business whose moat I can't verify is not a margin of safety, it's a question. Accenture sells people's time to clients, and the franchise rests on client relationships and the embedded nature of its work. I'm not at all sure AI and automation won't compress what clients pay for that labor over the next decade, and moats that must be rebuilt continuously are no moats at all. The snapshot also says nothing about ten years of earnings, ROIC, cash-flow quality or management, so I can't call the checklist complete. I'll put it on the watch list and wait until I can answer the durability question with confidence; waiting costs me nothing.

exit_trigger: Franchise test fails: ROE falls below 15% in more than 20% of reported fiscal years; Reported negative annual operating cash flow in any of the newest five fiscal years; Evidence of brand erosion: persistent discounting or loss of pricing power; Price above 1.5x intrinsic value, which is not close at $106.44 against the $363.03 model estimate; Discovery of dishonest reporting or value-destroying acquisitions by management
rationale: I own this one, and it is down 17.09% from my $128.38 entry after 101 days. A price decline is not a sell trigger when the franchise is intact. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 34.6% and a debt-to-equity of 0.0, which is the economics of a brand that earns high returns without borrowed money. The model's $363 per share rests on a 5% discount rate and 8% growth, and I would not bet the farm on a number that generous, but even a heavy haircut leaves a wide gap to $106.44. My real worry is the one Charlie would raise: athletic apparel is fashion-adjacent, and a brand that must be rebuilt every season is no moat at all. So I keep the shares, add nothing until I can verify the 10-year earnings record and management, and let the reported returns on capital tell me whether the brand holds.

exit_trigger: Moat erosion: ROE falls below 15% in more than 20% of fiscal years; Sustained negative operating cash flow, which would signal management or contract-execution failure; Loss of a major franchise program or a shift in Navy procurement that undermines its position; Price above 1.5x intrinsic value, if the gap persists
rationale: I can explain this business in two paragraphs: it builds warships for one dominant customer, the U.S. Navy, and there are very few places that customer can go. That is a regulatory-style moat, but a moat that comes from a single buyer's budget is not the same as a See's Candies brand, because the customer sets the terms. The snapshot shows a 45.7% margin of safety, but it rests on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, and I would want to haircut that for a shipbuilder with one customer. ROE of 15.26% and debt-to-equity of 0.49 only just clear my bars, with no cushion. The snapshot has no ten-year earnings record, no CEO tenure and no ROIC, so I cannot say the criteria are met. I don't own it, I have no pressing reason to buy it, and I will wait for the evidence.
